column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
A class sets up a stall at a festival and must decide on costs, prices and whether the day made money. What larger idea does this small exercise stand for?
Think of a person who makes eco-friendly bags to replace plastic ones. Which jobs do they carry out, from noticing the problem to helping society?
What did a group of women with almost no money use to build a large organisation, and how did they make sure everyone benefited fairly?
What bold step did the young clerk take to own a hotel, and which qualities beyond a good idea did his career show?
Before a group of friends open a shop, what could go wrong if they simply start without writing anything down?
For a new bakery, which questions about the people nearby and the money needed should be answered before ordering an oven?
A new shop must pick a place, a team and a price tag. What tests should each of those choices pass?
How do new shops let people know they exist, and what kinds of trouble should owners expect and plan for?
Why do firms split work into groups with distinct tasks, and what does the business gain when the groups work together?
In a bakery, which group decides the daily baking plan, which hires and trains helpers, and which draws in customers?
In a bakery, which spending stays the same even if no cake is sold, and which rises with every cake baked?
A shop takes in a month's money and pays all its bills. How do you tell whether the month ended in gain or loss, and what changes after tax?
Which kind of group was doing business long before the word startup, and how did they keep their skills alive?
What habits let this community lend without formal banks and keep growing, and what do they teach modern business owners?
If a young company folds after an honest effort, what value can the founder still take away?
Which people and policies are behind India's rise as a startup nation, and what national aims do these ventures serve?
